Suppose C\mathcal{C}C is finitely complete and F:C→DF : \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}F:C→D preserves binary products. I want to show that FFF preserves finite products.

I tried ternary products for a simple example. Take objects A,B,CA, B, CA,B,C in C\mathcal{C}C, and projections πA:P→A,πB:P→B,πC:P→C\pi_A : P \to A, \pi_B : P \to B, \pi_C : P \to CπA​:P→A,πB​:P→B,πC​:P→C that form a limit cone. We need to show that F(πA),F(πB),F(πC)F(\pi_A), F(\pi_B), F(\pi_C)F(πA​),F(πB​),F(πC​) form a limit cone.

I can think of a proof that does this but writing it out explicitly makes it seem… long-winded. What is the most efficient way to establish this result?

Ideally there’d be a result of the form “if F preserves this class of limits, and you can build up limit type X from iterated limits from this class, then F preserves limit type X”, but I’m not sure how to state “you can build up limit type X from iterated limits” precisely.

Right Kan extension along {0,...,n+1}→{0,...,n}\{0,...,n+1\} \to \{0,...,n\}{0,...,n+1}→{0,...,n} (where n+1n+1n+1 is mapped to nnn) can be computed pointwise from binary (and unary) products. If FFF preserves those, it preserves such Kan extensions, hence it preserves Kan extensions along the composite {0,...,n+1}→{0,...,n}→...→{0} \{0,...,n+1\} \to \{0,...,n\} \to ... \to \{0\}{0,...,n+1}→{0,...,n}→...→{0}, i.e. finite products.

So, "build up limit of type X from iterated limits" can be mean that limit of type X is a right Kan extension along a (finite) composite of Kan extensions computed pointwise from limits in the class.

Doesn't it work to argue as follows?

  • Having a finite product c1×⋯×cnc_1 \times \dots \times c_nc1​×⋯×cn​ is equivalent to having a natural iso [X,c1×⋯×cn]≅[X,c1]×⋯×[X,cn][X,c_1\times \dots \times c_n] \cong [X,c_1] \times \dots \times [X,c_n][X,c1​×⋯×cn​]≅[X,c1​]×⋯×[X,cn​]
  • We have natural isos
    [d,F(c1×c2×c3)]≅[d,F((c1×c2)×c3)]≅[d,F(c1×c2)]×[d,F(c3)]≅[d,F(c1)]×[d,F(c2)]×[d,F(c3)]\begin{array}{rcl} {[d, F(c_1 \times c_2 \times c_3)]} &\cong & [d, F((c_1 \times c_2) \times c_3)] \\ &\cong & [d, F(c_1 \times c_2)] \times [d,F(c_3)] \\ & \cong & [d, F(c_1)] \times [d,F(c_2)] \times [d, F(c_3)]\end{array}[d,F(c1​×c2​×c3​)]​≅≅≅​[d,F((c1​×c2​)×c3​)][d,F(c1​×c2​)]×[d,F(c3​)][d,F(c1​)]×[d,F(c2​)]×[d,F(c3​)]​
    (fixing some associativity default for ×\times× in sets).

So this argument works to show that binary products imply finite products. But you need a slightly different argument for showing preservation of binary products implies preservation of finite products. It’s not enough to show the requisite natural isomorphism, it has to be the “canonical” one.

The right kan extension argument is intriguing - it reminds me a bit of Paolo Perrone’s “Kan extensions are partial colimits” paper. Is that what’s happening here?

Ruby Khondaker (she/her) said:

It’s not enough to show the requisite natural isomorphism, it has to be the “canonical” one.

Ah, I see!
But the first claim above may be refined by adding that the projections are given by the image of the identity.
The proof shows that F(c1×⋯×cn)F(c_1\times\dots\times c_n)F(c1​×⋯×cn​) is a product whose projections are given by tracking down the image of the identity on F(c1×⋯×cn)F(c_1\times\dots\times c_n)F(c1​×⋯×cn​), which does give the images of projections in 𝒞𝒞C. Does this help convincing you? Am I missing something?

Yes this also works, but I found that it’s a little tedious to track the identity through the collection of natural isomorphisms to show it equals F applied to the projections, and moreso once you get to more complicated limit shapes.

It feels like there should be a result of the form “so long as the intermediate natural isos you use are canonical, then their composite is”, but I haven’t figured out a precise way to formulate this.

@El Mehdi Cherradi Your suggestion has helped me organise these ideas in my mind a little better! I was thinking about how to view this through the usual construction of limits from products and equalisers. What I've figured out is the following.

We start with a category J\mathcal{J}J. From this, we can make a "bipartite" category Bipartite(J)\text{Bipartite}(\mathcal{J})Bipartite(J) as follows. The collection of objects is Ob(J)∐Mor(J)\text{Ob}(\mathcal{J}) \coprod \text{Mor}(\mathcal{J})Ob(J)∐Mor(J). For each morphism f:j→j′f : j \to j'f:j→j′ in our original category, we add two morphisms to this new category - one from the object representing jjj to the object representing fff, and one from the object representing j′j'j′ to the object representing fff.

Then, there is an initial functor Bipartite(J)→J\text{Bipartite}(\mathcal{J}) \to \mathcal{J}Bipartite(J)→J which sends each object to itself and each morphism to its codomain. So to compute a limit of a diagram with shape J\mathcal{J}J, it suffices to compute the limit of the corresponding diagram with shape Bipartite(J)\text{Bipartite}(\mathcal{J})Bipartite(J).

Next, we have a functor Bipartite(J)→Eq\text{Bipartite}(\mathcal{J}) \to \text{Eq}Bipartite(J)→Eq, where Eq\text{Eq}Eq is the shape category used for equalisers. So long as our ambient category C\mathcal{C}C has products, we can pointwise right kan extend along this functor. This means it suffices to compute a limit of a diagram of shape Eq\text{Eq}Eq, an equaliser! Indeed, one can check that the pointwise right kan extension products a parallel pair with domain ∏j∈JD(j)\prod_{j \in \mathcal{J}} D(j)∏j∈J​D(j) and codomain ∏α∈mor(J)D(codα)\prod_{\alpha \in \text{mor}(\mathcal{J})} D(\text{cod} \alpha)∏α∈mor(J)​D(codα).

Finally, computing the limit of this equaliser is equivalent to right kan-extending along the canonical functor Eq→1\text{Eq} \to 1Eq→1.

So it seems that these various limit-reshaping operations fall into two types:
1) Restricting along an initial functor
2) (Pointwise) right kan-extending along another functor

The first type works in any category. If your category has limits of a certain shape, then you establish existence of such pointwise kan extensions and can then apply the second type. I believe this is a way to formalise making "iterated" limits to compute a larger limit?
